title: Shakuntala
hook: Shakuntala walks into the king's hall with his son, and he says he has never seen her before

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakuntala at the hermitage, saying yes to a king only on a promise spoken aloud.

A crowded royal hall, and a woman holding a boy by the hand. No one ever came from the city, so Kanva has sent Shakuntala and her son to the king. She bows and says it plainly: this is your son. Make him your heir, as you promised me at the hermitage. King Dushyanta looks at her and says he doesn't know her, never married her, has no idea who she is. Everyone is watching. What does she do now?
screen: `I DON'T REMEMBER YOU.` → `THIS IS YOUR SON.` → `EVERYONE IS WATCHING.`

segments.voice: For a moment, the epic says, she can't move. She stands there stunned, ashamed and furious at once, her eyes going red. Then she speaks, for a long time. Here is some of it, in paraphrase. First, witnesses. You think you're alone with what you did, she tells him, but the sun and the moon, the wind and fire, the earth and the sky, your own heart, all of them saw. You know, and you're saying you don't. Second, the boy. A son is his father born again; look at him and you see yourself, as if in a mirror. Third, when the king answers with insults about her mother the apsara and her birth in the forest, she turns his words around. You can see other people's faults when they're as small as a mustard seed, she says, and you can't see your own when they're as big as a bilva fruit. She never begs. She never pretends the promise was smaller than it was. She stands in a king's own hall and tells him the truth about himself. When he still refuses, she turns to go. Then a voice from the sky tells the king that she speaks the truth, and that the boy is his son. Only then does Dushyanta take them in. This is a week's end, so look back. The week began with Savitri remembered at a banyan. Then Damayanti, choosing the mortal, searching with a question, naming the wound. And now Shakuntala, in a hall full of people, refusing to be unknown.
screen: `STUNNED, THEN SHE SPEAKS` · `THE SUN AND MOON WERE WITNESSES` · `A MUSTARD SEED AND A BILVA FRUIT` · `A VOICE FROM THE SKY AGREES`

segments.voice: Feel the floor under your feet, the air on your skin, any light in the room, and let them be quiet witnesses to you sitting here, the way Shakuntala named the sun, the wind and the earth. Then let your own heart see you honestly, faults and all, without a verdict. If you pray, you can bring it into prayer.
Shakuntala. The woman who stood in a king's hall and told him the truth until the sky itself agreed.
Your line: Shakuntala. A mustard seed out there, a bilva fruit in here. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one, done.

howItsDone: Hindus know Shakuntala's speech at court from the Mahabharata's first book, the Adi Parva; the same story is retold in the poet Kalidasa's later play, which changes how the king comes to forget her.

fork.reveal: after a moment of stunned silence, she speaks at length: about witnesses, about the son as a mirror, about the faults he can't see. when he still refuses, a voice from the sky confirms her.

original.note: Sanskrit: the epic explains her name from shakunta, bird, for the birds that guarded her as a baby.

what a scholar hears: her speech calls the sun, moon, wind, fire, earth, sky and his own heart as witnesses, and only a voice from the sky ends the standoff.

chat.says: When the king said he didn't know her, what did Shakuntala do?
options: She spoke the truth in his hall: the sun, the wind and his own heart all saw.
She begged him quietly to remember her, then went back to the forest.
She said nothing at all, and waited for Kanva to come and prove it.
chat.meaning: She named the witnesses, the sun, moon, wind, earth and his own heart, and turned his insults around. She never begged.

Dushyanta.meaning: the king who says he doesn't know her

bilva.meaning: a large fruit, set here against a tiny mustard seed

apsara.meaning: a celestial dancer; Shakuntala's mother was one

Kanva.meaning: the sage who raised her and sent her to court

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Shakuntala at Dushyanta's court; his denial; her speech: the witnesses, the son as the father's self, the mustard seed and the bilva fruit; the king's insults; the voice from the sky)
